newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia lifts ban on new uranium deals with France.
newsitem.headline: Australia lifts ban on new uranium deals with France.

text.p: Australia on Monday lifted a ban on new uranium contracts with France in recognition of Paris's signing of a global nuclear test ban pact.
The move came as Aborigines in Australia's Northern Territory began a campaign to stop new uranium mines on their land.

"The government has decided to lift the ban on new uranium supply contracts with France in the light of the French signature of the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty on September 24," said Australian Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer.
The ban on new uranium contracts, which has proved costly to Australian producers, was imposed in 1988 when France ended a moratorium on nuclear tests in the Pacific.

"France's support for the treaty outlawing nuclear testing for all time reinforces other actions taken, since its announcement of a 'definitive end to nuclear testing' on January 29, which demonstrate a commitment to nuclear non-proliferation and disarmament objectives," Fischer said in a statement.
This included closing test sites and signing protocols to a South Pacific nuclear weapons-free zone treaty, he said.
France has emerged as one of the world's biggest markets for uranium after the country embraced nuclear power generation following the oil shocks of the 1970s.
Australian uranium miner Energy Resources of Australia Ltd (ERA) has described Electricite de France, the national power company, as the world's single largest buyer of uranium.
Fischer said the decision would be good news for the future of uranium mining at the Roxby Downs mine, owned by WMC Ltd and the Ranger mine, owned by ERA.
"It's going to be a boost for exports, it's a correct policy decision," Fischer told reporters.
Richard Yeeles, corporate affairs manager for WMC's copper-uranium division, said the company welcomed the decision but it was too early to speak about new contracts.
"It's a competitive market and any sales opportunities are going to depend on the utilities' requirements for uranium from Australia," he said.

Hours before the announcement, Aborigines opposed to a new uranium mine ERA is planning near the Kakadu National Park in the Northern Territory started a campaign to gain support from unions and environmentalists.
"Our community are fringe dwellers in the shadow of commercial gain," said Jacqui Katona, executive officer for the Gundjehmi Aboriginal Corporation.
"We have sacrificed country before, we cannot be asked to sacrifice again," Katona told a news conference in Sydney.

Aboriginal leaders from the three clans which cover the proposed Jabiluka mine site and ERA's existing Ranger uranium mine will tour Australia's main eastern states meeting with unions, environmental groups and politicians.
The Aboriginal leaders said they opposed any further uranium mining on their land because previous mines had brought social dislocation to their people.

"We have no desire to see any more country ripped up and further negative intrusions on our lives," said the leaders in a statement. "Our future depends on our culture remaining strong. Our cultural values cannot be traded for money."
They also said that any further mining would threaten the environmentally sensitive Kakadu National Park, which has been World Heritage listed by the Australian government.
"In 1978, this whole area was under water in the wet season," said Katona. "If there is a spill on a road, they can't guarantee they can clean it up."
